# MIDI to MCU: Teaching the Roland MC-500mkII to Drive Your DAW

The Roland MC-500mkII is a multitrack tape machine for MIDI. It has good buttons. It does not, by itself, talk to your DAW.

I built a small service that bridges the gap. The MC-500mkII speaks MIDI Song Position Pointer and start/stop/continue; the DAW speaks Mackie Control Universal. The service translates between them.

---

## What it is

A bridge process that runs on your laptop. It opens a CoreMIDI virtual port on the input side, listens to the MC-500mkII over MIDI, and emits MCU transport messages to your DAW on the output side.

The MC-500mkII becomes a transport controller. Hit play on the MC-500, the DAW plays. Hit stop, it stops. Spin the data wheel, the DAW jogs. Pre-configure a location memory, recall it, and the DAW seeks there.

```
MC-500mkII  →  bridge  →  MCU  →  DAW
   (MIDI)              (CoreMIDI virtual port)
```

---

## What's tested

**Hardware.** Roland MC-500mkII · 1988 · 8-track · Super MRC OS. The Super MRC OS is the load-bearing requirement — the original 1986 MC-500 doesn't expose the timing and locate semantics the bridge depends on. The Roland MC-50 (1989, similar architecture, smaller form factor, cheaper) probably works but I haven't verified.

**DAWs.** Logic Pro, Ableton Live, LUNA. The bridge emits standard MCU; in theory any DAW that accepts an MCU controller should work. I'm only claiming the three I've run end-to-end.

**Platform.** macOS via CoreMIDI. The Linux build uses ALSA virtual ports — that path compiles and runs, but I haven't put it against a real DAW.

---

## What you get from the panel

The MC-500mkII panel maps to the DAW transport one-for-one. Stop, play, record, fast-forward, rewind. The data wheel becomes a jog wheel — fine resolution when you turn it slowly, faster scrub when you spin.

Location memories are the interesting part. The MC-500mkII stores 99 location markers in NVRAM. The bridge maps each to an MCU `LOCATE` message, so pre-configured locations on the MC-500 jump the DAW to the corresponding bar and beat. Practical use: store the verse, chorus, and bridge of a session as MC-500 locations. The MC-500's panel becomes a tactile arrangement-jumping interface for whatever DAW is on the other end.

---

## How it works

SPP carries 14-bit MIDI beat positions at 1/16-note resolution. The bridge converts SPP to MTC at the DAW's session sample rate, then wraps the position in an MCU `GOTO` so the DAW seeks. Start, stop, and continue map to MCU transport directly.

The jog wheel arrives as MIDI controller data. The bridge translates it into MCU jog-wheel deltas, scaled to the DAW's frame rate.

The MIDI port the bridge listens on is a virtual CoreMIDI port that any DAW can connect to as an MCU surface — no driver, no kernel extension, no DAW plugin.

---

## Get it

The bridge ships from the `audiocontrol-org/audiocontrol` releases page:

- Pre-compiled binaries for macOS and Linux
- Homebrew formula
- macOS `.app` — drag it into `/Applications/`. No terminal required.

→ Releases: <https://github.com/audiocontrol-org/audiocontrol/releases>
→ Source: <https://github.com/audiocontrol-org/audiocontrol>

---

## What's next

The MC-50 needs verification. Windows isn't compiled yet. The MCU surface I cover is transport, jog, and locate; channel selection and v-pot mappings are the next reasonable bits to handle.

If you have an MC-500mkII and a DAW, try it. If it breaks on your setup, file an issue with the platform and DAW version.
